title: Beneath the Surface of Words Are the Foundations for Life
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos argues that morphology instruction and phonics can coexist in literacy teaching, and that the Structured Word Inquiry community wrongly dismisses early phonics. She leans on Linnea Ehri and David Share, who hold that the alphabetic principle must come first, and on morphology-focused practitioners Sue Hegland and Lyn Stone, who value phonics while insisting morphology is not an add-on. Her move is to set these figures against Peter and Jeffrey Bowers, whom she faults for failing to say that phonics is necessary but not sufficient and for lacking a classroom-ready scope and sequence. She proposes keeping efficient linguistic phonics for beginners while displaying high-utility word families during writing time. The post ends with a plea that research and logic, rather than ideology, guide how beginning reading is sequenced.
points: Ehri and Share both treat the simplified basic code as a necessary starting model, which Janetos uses to argue beginning reading should start with the most transparent spellings.

She faults the Bowers brothers for not acknowledging that phonics is necessary but not sufficient, for not distinguishing efficient from inefficient programs, and for lacking a classroom-ready SWI scope and sequence.
Hegland and Stone are held up as the model of balance because they affirm phonics for beginners while treating morphology as integral at every stage.
Her practical suggestion is to keep phonics for the reading block and introduce high-utility morphological word families like play, plays, played, playing during writing time.
The closing claim is that schools should be guided by research and then logic, not ideology, so the sequence of instruction fits what beginners can handle.
quotes: Teaching the alphabetic principle is fundamental and gets the ball rolling. To draw attention to plural suffixes, students need to know the shape of the letter S, named “ess” and that it can represent /s/ or /z/.
You’ve got to give kids a model they can work with, and then with time and experience they will expand their knowledge. The branches will grow and the leaves will be added.

By contrast, Sue and Lyn openly acknowledge the limited but useful purpose of a well-functioning phonics program—understanding both its promise and its peril. They establish its utility but repeatedly refer to its limitations and warn against its excesses so that morphology isn’t called upon to mop up on Aisle P as needed but is featured prominently in its own right.

We can deliberately start with the most regular and transparent spellings without feeling ingenuine or duplicitous. Basically, teachers cultivate (to borrow Share’s tree metaphor) a locally transparent orthography—attaching (to shift to a mechanical metaphor) training wheels to the reading bike—that allow children to master the alphabetic principle before encountering the broader morphological and orthographic complexity of English.

We are asked to sacrifice the sequencing of the alphabetic code on the altar of the truth of our language as if linguistic truth trumps tried-and-true teaching methods. We are in school—not church—which means the only truth we traffic in is the one that is informed by research, and when research is lacking, then we look to logic, not ideology, to guide us.

If you stand with both common sense and science—with renowned professors as well as experienced practitioners—to allow morphology instruction to peacefully coexist with phonics, your students will thank you for it. I thank Sue, Lyn, and Sean for it.
